aim.title: The aim
aim.text: Attract birds to your forest, grassland and wetland. Every bird you place makes that habitat's action stronger, so your board grows into an engine. After 4 rounds, the player with the most points wins.

setup.title: Setup
setup.text: Each player starts with 5 random bird cards in hand and 1 of each food (🌾 seed, 🐛 insect, 🐟 fish, 🍒 fruit, 🐭 rodent). Three bird cards are laid face up in the bird tray; the rest form the deck. Four round goals are drawn, one for each round.

board.title: Your board
board.text: Your board has three habitat rows with 5 slots each. The button at the start of a row is that habitat's action, and its ×N shows how much it gives right now. It starts small and grows by 1 for every 2 birds in that row.
board.strength: How much each action gives, by the number of birds in its row:
board.slots: Playing a bird also costs eggs, depending on the slot. You take them from any of your birds:

cards.title: Bird cards
cards.points: Points (top right): scored at the end of the game.
cards.cost: Food cost: what you pay to play the bird. ❔ means any food of your choice.
cards.habitats: Habitats: the 🌲 🌼 💧 icons show where the bird can live.
cards.eggLimit: Egg limit (🥚 × N): the most eggs the bird can hold.
cards.power: Power (⚡, on some birds): a bonus that triggers when you use its habitat's action.

turn.title: Your turn
turn.text: Players take turns one after another. On your turn, take exactly one of these four actions:
turn.playBird: Play a bird: choose a bird from your hand, pay its food cost, and place it in the leftmost empty slot of a habitat it can live in. The first two slots of a row are free; slots 3 and 4 also cost 1 egg, and slot 5 costs 2 eggs. You can take the eggs from any of your birds, and you choose which food pays for each ❔. You can't play a bird into a full row, or into a slot whose egg cost you can't pay.
turn.gainFood: 🌲 Gain food: take 1 food of your choice, plus 1 more for every 2 birds in your forest. You can mix types or take several of the same one. The food supply never runs out.
turn.layEggs: 🌼 Lay eggs: lay 2 eggs, plus 1 more for every 2 birds in your grassland, spread over any of your birds as you like. A bird can't hold more than its egg limit. You must lay all of them while you have room; if your birds run out of room, you lay fewer.
turn.drawCards: 💧 Draw cards: take 1 card, plus 1 more for every 2 birds in your wetland. Mix the face-up tray and the top of the deck however you like. If fewer cards are left, you take what there is. There is no hand limit.
turn.after: After a habitat action (gain food, lay eggs or draw cards), the birds in that row use their powers (see below).

powers.title: Bird powers
powers.text: When you use a habitat's action, every bird in that row with a power (⚡) activates it, from right to left. Powers happen automatically:
powers.gainFood: Gain food: you gain 1 food of the type shown.
powers.layEggSelf: Lay an egg on this bird: 1 egg goes on the bird itself, if it has room.
powers.layEggAny: Lay an egg on any bird: 1 egg goes on whichever of your birds has the most room.
powers.drawCard: Draw a card: you draw 1 card from the deck.
powers.allGainFood: Everyone gains food: every player, including your opponents, gains 1 food of the type shown.

notes.ownTurn: Powers only work on your own turn, when you take that habitat's action. Playing a bird doesn't trigger its power: it joins in the next time you use its row.
notes.extra: Powers come on top of the action: for example, Lay eggs ×3 with a lay-an-egg bird in your grassland gives you 4 eggs.
notes.skipped: A power that can't happen is skipped: the bird is full, all your birds are full, or the deck is empty.

deck.title: Bird tray and deck
deck.copies: The deck has two copies of every bird, shuffled at the start of the game.
deck.refill: At the end of every turn, empty spaces in the tray are refilled from the top of the deck.
deck.newRound: At the start of each new round, the cards in the tray are removed from the game and three new cards are laid out.
deck.empty: When the deck runs out, the tray isn't refilled any more. If fewer cards are left than you would draw, you take the rest.

rounds.title: Rounds and goals
rounds.text: The game lasts 4 rounds. Each player gets 8 turns in round 1, 7 in round 2, 6 in round 3 and 5 in round 4, so every action counts for more as the game goes on. A round ends when every player has used all their turns. Each new round starts with a fresh bird tray, and the next player in turn order goes first.
rounds.goals: At the end of each round, that round's goal (shown at the top of the screen) is scored. Whoever has the most of it comes 1st, the next player 2nd:
rounds.ties: You need at least 1 to place. Tied players share the points of the places they take, rounded down: if two players tie for 1st, they split the 1st and 2nd place points.
rounds.tieExample: Example in round {{round}} ({{first}} and {{second}} points): if two players tie for the most, each gets {{split}} ({{first}} + {{second}}, halved and rounded down) and nobody comes 2nd. If two players tie behind a clear leader, the leader gets {{first}} and the other two get {{half}} each.
rounds.goalList: Each game uses 4 of these 8 goals, so not all of them come up:
rounds.goalNotes: Only eggs on grassland birds count for “Most eggs in grassland”. Bird points are the points printed on the birds on your board, without eggs.
rounds.solo: Playing solo, you take 1st place in every goal where you have at least 1, so the challenge is to beat your own best score.

end.title: End of the game
end.birds: Bird points: the points of every bird on your board.
end.food: Leftover food: 1 point per food, up to 5.
end.tie: The highest total wins. If it's a tie, the player with more leftover food wins; if that's tied too, they share the win.

tips.title: Tips
tips.engine: Early on, play birds into the habitat you use most: a stronger action pays off on every turn after.
tips.powers: A bird's power pays off every time you use its row, so power birds are worth playing early.
tips.eggs: Eggs are worth points, but you also need them to fill the later slots of a row.
tips.food: Leftover food is worth at most 5 points, so spend the rest before the game ends.
tips.lastRound: In the last round, laying eggs is often worth more than starting something new.
tips.goals: Keep an eye on the next round's goal and plan for it.

welcome.title: Welcome, {{name}}!
welcome.body: Over 4 rounds you attract birds to your forest, grassland and wetland. On each turn you take exactly one action. Here is a quick look around.

hand.title: Your hand
hand.body: Each card shows the bird’s points (top right), food cost, the habitats it can live in and its egg limit. Drag a playable bird onto a matching habitat row to play it, or click it to choose the details.

food.title: Your food
food.body: Birds are paid for with food from here. ❔ on a card means any food. Leftover food is worth 1 point each at the end (up to 5).

board.title: Your board
board.body: Three habitats with 5 slots each. Birds fill a row from left to right; slots 3–5 also cost eggs, shown in the empty slot.

actions.title: Habitat actions
actions.body: Instead of playing a bird, use a habitat: 🌲 gain food, 🌼 lay eggs, 💧 draw cards. Every 2 birds in a row make its action stronger, and those birds then use their powers, right to left.

tray.title: The bird tray
tray.body: Face-up cards and the deck. Drag them into your hand (or click them) to draw: that’s the wetland action.

goals.title: Round goals
goals.body: Each round ends with a goal. The leaders score bonus points, more in later rounds. A round ends when everyone has used their turns.

panel.title: Your choices
panel.body: Whatever you start appears here: pick the details and press Confirm. Score points with birds, eggs, leftover food and goals. Good luck!

birdFacts.american-robin: North America's most abundant land bird. It was named after the European robin for its orange-red breast, though the two aren't closely related. Often seen tugging earthworms out of lawns.
birdFacts.barn-owl: Easy to recognise by its pale, heart-shaped face. Barn owls are among the most widespread birds on Earth and hunt mice and voles at night, largely by sound.
birdFacts.blue-jay: A noisy, crested relative of crows in bright blue, white and black. It buries acorns to eat later, and the forgotten ones help oak forests spread.
birdFacts.northern-cardinal: The male is bright red with a black face mask; the female is olive-brown with red accents. This crested songbird is the state bird of seven US states.
birdFacts.black-capped-chickadee: A tiny tit with a black cap and bib, named after its 'chick-a-dee-dee-dee' call. It hides food for winter, and the part of its brain that remembers the hiding places grows in caching season.
birdFacts.downy-woodpecker: The smallest woodpecker in North America, only 14–18 cm long. It nests in tree holes and eats mostly insects, and looks almost identical to the larger hairy woodpecker.
birdFacts.pileated-woodpecker: A crow-sized woodpecker with a flaming red crest, the largest in North America. It chisels big, almost rectangular holes into trees to reach ants and other insects.
birdFacts.great-horned-owl: A big owl with feathered 'horns' (ear tufts), nicknamed the 'tiger of the air'. It hunts rabbits and rodents and is one of the few regular predators of skunks.
birdFacts.cedar-waxwing: A sleek brown, grey and yellow bird. Some wing feathers end in red tips that look like drops of sealing wax, which gives it its name. It lives largely on berries.
birdFacts.ruby-throated-hummingbird: Eastern North America's most common hummingbird; the male has a glittering red throat. On migration this tiny bird crosses the Gulf of Mexico without stopping.
birdFacts.wild-turkey: The heaviest of the chicken-like birds and the wild ancestor of the domestic turkey. Despite its bulk it flies well over short distances and sleeps in trees.
birdFacts.red-tailed-hawk: One of North America's most common hawks, living everywhere from deserts to cities. Adults have a brick-red tail, and its raspy scream is often used for eagles in films.
birdFacts.wood-duck: One of North America's most colourful waterfowl. It nests in tree holes, and the ducklings leap to the ground the day after hatching.
birdFacts.bald-eagle: The national bird of the United States: a sea eagle that snatches fish from the water with its talons. It builds the largest tree nests ever recorded, up to 4 m deep and a tonne in weight.
birdFacts.american-kestrel: The smallest and most common falcon in the Americas, about the size of a blue jay. It hovers over fields before dropping onto insects and small rodents.
birdFacts.eastern-bluebird: A small thrush: the male's bright blue back and rusty breast make it a birdwatchers' favourite. It nests in tree holes and nest boxes and is the state bird of Missouri and New York.
birdFacts.western-meadowlark: A ground-nesting grassland bird with a yellow breast and a black 'V' necklace. Its flute-like song is so loved that six US states chose it as their state bird.
birdFacts.mourning-dove: One of North America's most abundant birds, named for its soft, sad-sounding coo. Its wings whistle on take-off, and a pair can raise up to six broods a year.
birdFacts.house-sparrow: Carried around the globe by people, it is the most widely distributed wild bird. It lives almost wherever humans do, in cities and on farms alike.
birdFacts.barn-swallow: The world's most widespread swallow, recognisable by its long, deeply forked tail. It builds a cup of mud for a nest, usually inside barns and other buildings.
birdFacts.killdeer: A plover named after its shrill 'kill-deer' call. To lure predators away from its nest, it pretends to have a broken wing and drags it along the ground.
birdFacts.greater-prairie-chicken: A grouse famous for its 'booming' courtship: males inflate orange air sacs on their necks to make a deep hooting sound. Once abundant, it is now rare due to habitat loss.
birdFacts.burrowing-owl: A small, long-legged owl that lives underground, usually in burrows dug by prairie dogs or ground squirrels. Unlike most owls, it is often active during the day.
birdFacts.red-winged-blackbird: Males are glossy black with red-and-yellow shoulder patches that they flash while singing from cattails. Possibly North America's most numerous land bird, it winters in flocks of over a million.
birdFacts.great-blue-heron: A large, patient wading bird that stands still in shallow water to spear fish. An all-white form in Florida and the Caribbean is called the great white heron.
birdFacts.mallard: The ancestor of most domestic ducks, found across the Northern Hemisphere. Drakes have glossy green heads, females are speckled brown, and both have a blue wing patch.
birdFacts.belted-kingfisher: A shaggy-crested kingfisher that dives headfirst for fish. Unusually, the female is more colourful than the male, with an extra rusty belly band. It nests in tunnels dug into riverbanks.
birdFacts.osprey: A fish-hunting raptor found on every continent except Antarctica. It plunges feet-first into the water and can turn one toe backwards to grip slippery fish.
birdFacts.common-loon: A large diving bird of northern lakes, with a black-and-white chequered back in summer. Its haunting, yodelling call is a classic sound of the North American wilderness.
birdFacts.american-white-pelican: A huge white pelican that doesn't dive: groups herd fish into the shallows together and scoop them up. In breeding season a horn-like plate grows on its bill.
birdFacts.sandhill-crane: A tall grey crane with a red forehead, named after Nebraska's Sandhills. Up to 450,000 gather along the Platte River on their spring migration.
birdFacts.snowy-egret: A small white heron with black legs and bright yellow feet. Its fine plumes were once so prized for hats that it was nearly wiped out; legal protection let it recover.
